research_question: Can the modal fixity objection to eternalist reconciliations of divine foreknowledge and libertarian freedom be answered by adding a premise about the logical posteriority or cross-world contingency of God's eternal knowledge, or does eternal fixity remain incompatible with the power to do otherwise?

challenged_premise.text: Positing God as eternal, with all time present to Him, best respects both divine foreknowledge and libertarian free will.

objection: Sarah faces a choice at T2: she can help a stranger or walk past. God is eternal, with all moments present to Him, so God perceives Sarah walking past at T2—not as a prediction but as a present, completed reality within His timeless awareness. God's eternal perception is fixed and unalterable; it encompasses the entire timeline as one undivided whole. Now Sarah at T2 deliberates. For libertarian freedom, it must be within Sarah's power to help instead. But if Sarah were to help, God's eternal perception would have included her helping—which it does not. Since God's perception is eternally complete and cannot be otherwise, Sarah cannot do otherwise than what God perceives. The fixity is not removed; it is made permanent. Compare open theism: God knows all real possibilities but not which choice Sarah will make, leaving her future genuinely open. This alternative better respects libertarian freedom, since Sarah's choice remains undetermined by any prior or eternal fact.

strongest_responses.response: Defender A invoked the Grounding Principle to argue that God's eternal perception tracks rather than constrains the creature's choice, distinguishing the fixity of a known truth from the fixity of the act itself, and appealed to the Anselmian thesis to maintain that open options remain.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: The objector showed that counterfactual dependence does not establish that both options remain open at the moment of choice, and Defender A conceded that the Grounding Principle alone does not resolve the modal fixity objection without an additional premise about logical posteriority.

strongest_responses.response: Defender B recast the entailment as a harmless internal necessity and appealed to logical priority within God's single eternal act to make God's knowledge a consequence rather than a cause of the creature's decision.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: The objector demonstrated that grounding and logical priority are explanatory rather than modal relations, and that an eternally fixed perception combined with the entailment 'If God perceives P, then P' still appears to necessitate the act; Defender B conceded that an explicit contingency premise across possible worlds is required to avoid fatalism.

open_questions: Does the addition of a logical-posteriority or cross-world contingency premise genuinely dissolve the modal fixity objection, or does it merely relocate the problem by treating God's eternal knowledge as a necessary consequence of an act that still appears fixed from the eternal perspective?

Can the eternalist maintain that God's knowledge is immutable within any single possible world while also granting that the creature has the power to actualize a different world, without collapsing the distinction between God's knowledge and a necessary determinant of the act?

Is the distinction between explanatory grounding and modal fixity stable when God's eternal perception presents every temporal moment as an undivided whole, or does the eternal perspective inevitably undermine the openness required by libertarian freedom?
paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the modal fixity objection to eternalist reconciliations of divine foreknowledge and libertarian freedom can be answered by supplementing the Grounding Principle with a premise about the logical posteriority and cross-world contingency of God's eternal knowledge. The case would develop the defenders' revised claims—that God's eternal perception is grounded in the creature's choice and, though immutable within any single possible world, is contingent across possible worlds on that free choice—to show that eternal fixity is the consequence rather than the constraint of the creature's act. The strongest reply to anticipate is the objector's charge that grounding and logical priority are explanatory rather than modal relations, so that an eternally unalterable perception which necessarily entails the act still removes the power to do otherwise at the moment of choice. The paper would need to show that logical posteriority within God's eternal act genuinely leaves the creature's options open at T2 rather than merely redescribing a fixed eternal fact, and that the appeal to cross-world contingency does not presuppose the libertarian conclusion it is meant to defend.

reasons.coherence: The objection runs together the necessity of the consequence ('if God perceives P, then P') with the necessity of the act. Its open-theist comparison also fails to bear on the comparative premise as stated, since open theism gives up exhaustive foreknowledge, so it cannot 'better respect both'. The proposed paper is at least clearly aimed at the fixity worry.
reasons.robustness: The direction names the decisive reply (that grounding is explanatory, not modal) but gives no strategy for meeting it, and both defenders conceded the point in the trial. The paper as planned therefore has no worked answer to the standard transfer formulation.
reasons.significance: If it only adds logical posteriority and cross-world contingency, it would reproduce the classical Boethian/Anselmian position and Rogers' existing view; only a new argument against the fixity of eternity, or against transfer, would move the debate.
reasons.specificity: There is a definite thesis and a named reply to anticipate, but no account of which premise of the fixity argument is denied or how, and the literature base is largely irrelevant to the actual debate.

assessment.strongest_objection: The proposed supplement, that God's eternal knowledge is logically posterior to and contingent across worlds on the creature's choice, is not new. It restates the Boethian and Anselmian distinction between necessity of the consequence and necessity of the consequent, which Rogers (the author being defended) already deploys. The live problem since Pike, Plantinga, Zagzebski and Hasker is a transfer argument. It runs: (i) God's timeless belief is as fixed, or 'accidentally necessary', as a past fact; (ii) that belief strictly entails the act; (iii) necessity transfers across entailment (Rule Beta). The proposal never says which of these it rejects. Cross-world contingency answers none of them, because the incompatibilist grants that God's belief varies across worlds and still claims it is fixed relative to Sarah at T2. Without denying (i) or (iii), the paper only restates a reply the literature already holds to be insufficient.
assessment.what_it_needs: It must explicitly target one premise of the Zagzebski/Hasker timeless-knowledge transfer argument and defend that denial on independent grounds. One route is to deny that eternal facts are fixed relative to temporal agents, as a kind of 'soft fact'. The other is to reject Rule Beta for the relevant modality. It must also engage Rogers' own Anselmian account and the standard literature (Pike, Plantinga's 'On Ockham's Way Out', Zagzebski 1991, Hasker 1989, Stump and Kretzmann, Leftow, Fischer) rather than the tangential sources listed.
assessment.summary: This restates the traditional eternalist reply without confronting the timeless-knowledge transfer argument that defines the current debate. It is not publishable until it commits to rejecting a specific premise of that argument and defends that rejection.

revision.research_question: Can the timeless-knowledge transfer argument be blocked by denying its first premise, that God's eternal belief is fixed relative to a temporal agent like an accidentally necessary past fact, on independent grounds, or does eternal fixity remain incompatible with the power to do otherwise?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the transfer argument (Pike, Plantinga's 'On Ockham's Way Out', Zagzebski 1991, Hasker 1989) can be blocked by denying its first premise, that God's timeless belief is as fixed relative to Sarah at T2 as a past fact is. The paper abandons the earlier supplement of logical posteriority and cross-world contingency, because that move leaves premises (i) and (iii) untouched and so restates the Boethian and Anselmian position already held to be insufficient. The denial rests on the Grounding Principle (c007): the truth of God's belief depends on the actual choice, so the belief is not a hard fact that obtains independently of the agent's options at the time of choice. The paper defends this with a distinction between hard and soft facts. A soft fact is one whose unalterability relative to an agent is itself counterfactually dependent on that agent's act. Eternal beliefs are soft in this sense. The paper supports this with c019: the belief cannot be fixed at an earlier time, since S cannot be choosing before he is choosing. Rule Beta is granted in its proper modal scope, but it transfers necessity only from hard facts. The paper engages Rogers' Anselmian account on this point, using the open-options thesis (c006) as the test the soft-fact denial must meet. The conclusion is conditional: if the soft-fact denial can be independently motivated, eternalist reconciliation survives the transfer argument. If it cannot, the paper concedes that eternal fixity is incompatible with the power to do otherwise. Stump and Kretzmann, Leftow and Fischer serve as the standard rivals against which the soft-fact account is tested. The open-theist comparison is dropped, since open theism gives up exhaustive foreknowledge and cannot better respect both desiderata.
revision.reply_to_strongest_objection: The referee is right that cross-world contingency and posteriority concede premises (i) and (iii) and so do not answer the transfer argument. The paper therefore denies premise (i). It argues that God's timeless belief is a soft fact relative to Sarah at T2: its unalterability holds only given her act, and it inherits that status through the Grounding Principle (c007). Rule Beta is granted, but it transfers necessity only from hard facts that do not depend on the agent's options. Independent support comes from c019, which shows the belief cannot be fixed at a time before the choice. The paper's claim is that Sarah's power to help is a power over the act, whose counterfactual dependence includes the belief. It does not require that she now alter a fact independent of her act. Whether this is a motivated distinction or an ad hoc relabelling is the decisive test.
revision.what_changed: The revision replaces the cross-world posteriority supplement with a denial of the transfer argument's first premise, defended through a hard/soft fact distinction grounded in the Grounding Principle and c019.

reasons.coherence: The paper targets the transfer argument's fixity premise, but c025 is a comparative claim ('best respects'), and dropping the open-theist comparison leaves that comparison unaddressed; it also misuses c019, since a timeless belief was never 'fixed at an earlier time' anyway.
reasons.robustness: Its decisive move, counterfactual softness grounded in the Grounding Principle, faces the hard-type soft fact objection and a circularity charge, and the paper does not answer either; it only names 'motivated vs. ad hoc' as the test and offers no motivation beyond the explanatory grounding the trial already found modally inert.
reasons.significance: Even if it succeeded, it would mostly restate the Plantinga/Ockhamist line in eternalist dress, a modest refinement of a debate that Zagzebski, Hasker, Fischer and Rogers have already worked through extensively.
reasons.specificity: It has a definite target premise, named rivals and a conditional conclusion, but the crucial step (independent motivation for the soft-fact classification) is left as an open question, not a plan.

assessment.strongest_objection: This is Ockhamism moved into eternity, and it inherits Ockhamism's best-known problem. Zagzebski (1991) and Fischer showed that God's beliefs are 'hard-type soft facts.' A belief held by an essentially infallible God is a real intrinsic state of God, and that state is fixed whatever its entailments are. Defining softness as 'unalterability counterfactually dependent on the agent's act' assumes the very thing in dispute, namely that Sarah could have acted otherwise. Unless the paper explains why God's eternal belief-state, as opposed to the proposition it entails, is not fixed relative to Sarah, the proposal just relabels the fact.
assessment.what_it_needs: It must give a criterion of soft facts that does not presuppose Sarah's alternative possibilities, and apply it to God's eternal belief-state, not only to its propositional content, while answering Zagzebski's argument that eternity has its own necessity analogous to the past. It must also explain why this route belongs to eternalism specifically, rather than being generic Ockhamism that would work just as well for temporal foreknowledge.
assessment.summary: A competent restatement of Ockhamist eternalism that runs straight into the hard-type soft fact objection without an answer; it is not yet a paper, and it needs a non-question-begging criterion of softness specific to timeless belief before it is worth writing.
